extracted.intended_audience: OMB officials and federal agency regulatory analysts (those preparing and reviewing regulatory cost–benefit and distributional analyses)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for how federal agencies should disaggregate, quantify, and incorporate the distributional (demographic/subgroup) costs and benefits of proposed regulations into regulatory impact analyses and decisionmaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide demographically disaggregated totals
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should provide demographically disaggregated totals—in addition to aggregate calculations of costs and benefits—that evaluate how both positive and adverse regulatory impacts are distributed across specified subpopulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disaggregated estimates enable assessment of whether a rule is more or less net-beneficial for particular groups, help understand magnitude of distributional consequences (benefits, costs, and net benefits), allow assessment across the regulatory system (offsets or compounding effects), and can be reported regularly (e.g., yearly) to inform future actions and public engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: OMB should issue detailed methodology guidance for distributional analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB should prepare guidance recommending methodologies for disaggregating and monetizing benefits and costs and provide guidelines on the demographic subpopulations that agency analyses should consider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance should cover recommended methods for disaggregating/monetizing both benefits and costs, list subpopulations to consider, and provide step-by-step implementation instructions. It should be broad enough to cover environmental and non-environmental regulations and promote consistency across agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use granular scientific and demographic data to disaggregate benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysts should incorporate scientific and demographic data to measure benefits at a granular scale (geographic and demographic) using mapping, exposure data, and baseline vulnerability information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's 2016 technical guidance on environmental justice is a useful starting point; finer-scale air quality, health, and socioeconomic data allow assessment of pollution impacts across key population groups. Regular use of state-of-the-art air transport models and census demographic data is feasible in most contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use bounding analysis when detailed models are unavailable
rubrics_metrics.description: When similar analytical models are not readily available, analysts should perform a 'bounding analysis' that assumes that costs are passed on 'as changes in prices, wages, and/or returns to capital in both the short and long runs.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare bounding scenarios using disaggregated data on product purchases, wages by occupation, demographic composition of consumers/labor force, etc., to shed light on potential distributional consequences and estimate net benefits even with limited data or resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetize health and welfare benefits consistently across demographic groups
rubrics_metrics.description: The most defensible approach is to use the same monetized values for health and welfare benefits across all demographic groups rather than using group-specific willingness-to-pay values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using constant values avoids systematically undervaluing low-income groups (whose willingness to pay is bounded by income) and is consistent with regulatory precedent (e.g., EPA's use of a constant value of a statistical life). OMB should provide clear guidance endorsing constant monetizations across subpopulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disaggregate regulatory costs as well as benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should disaggregate the distribution of regulatory costs along demographic lines, not just benefits, because reporting only disaggregated health/environment effects may give an incomplete or biased picture of overall burdens faced by groups of concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cost distribution can be assessed using data on pass-through of compliance costs to consumers, the demographic makeup of the relevant consumer base and labor force, and other available cost data. OMB should expand guidance beyond environmental contexts to cover cost considerations across domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify a manageable default list of subpopulations to analyze
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB should identify a manageable list of demographic subpopulations that agency analyses should consider, balancing comprehensiveness with feasibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider factors such as prominence of indicators in equity concerns, data availability, and compatibility with quantitative tools. Executive orders highlight income and race; other characteristics (age, health status) may also be relevant. Preserve flexibility to consider additional groups qualitatively or quantitatively on a case-by-case basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise caution when using race-based data
rubrics_metrics.description: While disaggregated data based on race can inform racial or environmental justice impacts, agencies should be cautious about factoring race into regulatory decisionmaking because it may implicate constitutional issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal government should engage stakeholders when identifying which groups to consider; recommendations on specific groups are outside the report's scope. OMB may advise agencies to balance informational value with legal constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide step-by-step guidance on incorporating distributional analysis into decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB should provide agencies with step-by-step instructions on how to implement an approach for using distributional analysis and assess the magnitude or significance of distributional consequences relative to other effects (monetized costs/benefits and nonmonetized effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance should make explicit the value judgments involved and stress transparency about those judgments; it should be developed via a consultative process with stakeholder input on presentation and usage of distributional results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Option 1 — Qualitative incorporation of distributional findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies could qualitatively assess the desirability of distributional outcomes from a disaggregated cost-benefit analysis, treating them like nonmonetized costs or benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this approach, agencies retain discretion to weigh distributional desirability against aggregate net benefits; quantitative disaggregated totals supply support but do not mandate weighting. Agencies should 'exercise professional judgment' in determining importance of non-quantified or distributional effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Option 2 — Use standardized quantitative metrics (inequality metrics / scoring)
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB could recommend standardized quantitative metrics (inequality metrics or social welfare scoring functions) that enable regulators to 'score' distributional outcomes and present these alongside traditional cost-benefit analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These metrics would help rank and compare policy options by distributional effects; agencies would still have discretion in how to use scores when selecting alternatives. Examples include Gini coefficient, Atkinson index, and Theil index; prerequisite is having disaggregated impacts by subpopulations as per Recommendations 1–2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Option 3 — Weighted cost–benefit analysis integrating distributional outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies could fully integrate distributional effects into aggregate costs and benefits using distributional weights that reflect diminishing marginal utility of income (utilitarian) or prioritization of worst-off (prioritarian).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weighted CBA yields dollar-valued net benefits reflecting equity preferences and would replace traditional unweighted analyses. OMB should consult stakeholders to determine appropriate weighting approaches and whether to adopt utilitarian or prioritarian frameworks (or neither).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequality metrics: Gini coefficient, Atkinson index, Theil index
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific inequality metrics OMB could suggest: Gini (0–1, higher = more inequality), Atkinson (0–1, incorporates inequality-aversion parameter), Theil (0–infinity, higher = more inequality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metrics can be applied to distributions of impacts (e.g., exposure, benefits) rather than just income. Each has strengths/caveats: Atkinson incorporates normative judgments via aversion parameter; Theil may lack intuitive appeal and is often used alongside other metrics. Analysts must choose reference groups, relative vs absolute measures, ordinal vs nominal grouping, and any weighting choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisites and choices when using inequality metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Using inequality metrics requires prior disaggregation of impacts by subpopulation and making methodological choices about reference groups, relative vs absolute measures, group definitions (ordinal vs nominal), and weighting/value judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metrics are interpretable only when accounting for baseline inequality and evaluated alongside other benefits. Analysts should document choices and evaluate metrics in conjunction with aggregate monetized impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social welfare functions (SWFs) and weighting approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies could apply weights derived from Social Welfare Functions (e.g., utilitarian or prioritarian weights) to disaggregated costs and benefits to proxy different SWFs and rank policy options by distributional desirability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utilitarian weights reflect diminishing marginal utility of income (a dollar is worth more to a low-income person); prioritarian weights give greater value to improvements for the worse-off. SWFs typically use income/consumption but could use other well-being measures (health, leisure), which requires additional measurement steps and stakeholder consultation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency, stakeholder consultation, and public presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB should use a consultative process and public input to decide which approach(es) to recommend and how to present distributional results and underlying data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public engagement helps stakeholders and community groups benefit from access to distributional analyses. Any approach requires explicit value judgments; transparency about those judgments is key to consistent and robust distributional analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use inequality metrics alongside traditional cost–benefit analysis (not mandatory endorsement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pending stakeholder input, OMB should consider inequality metrics as one set of available tools for agencies to incorporate distributional analysis into decisionmaking, while not endorsing any single metric by default.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present inequality scores with disaggregated costs/benefits so regulators can contextualize distributional effects alongside other impacts; treat the outputs as informative inputs rather than decisive prescriptions absent policy choices about weighting.
